title: Rupee Crashes to 95.63, Worst Ever, as Oil Prices Spike
excerpt: US-Iran tensions, $105 crude, and $20 billion in foreign fund exits push India’s currency to uncharted territory
body:
The Indian rupee plunged to a record low of 95.63 against the US dollar on May 12, marking its steepest single-week slide in over two years as a toxic cocktail of geopolitical risk and commodity shock battered emerging-market sentiment.

**The Trigger:** President Trump’s dismissal of Iran’s latest peace proposal as a *‘piece of garbage’* sent Brent crude surging past $105 a barrel, a level not seen since late 2022. India, which imports roughly 85% of its oil, bore the brunt. The rupee had already weakened to 95.28 a day earlier; by Monday’s close, it had blown through that floor to 95.63, a full 6.5% decline year-to-date.

Foreign portfolio investors have yanked an estimated $20.6 billion from Indian equities since the start of 2026, accelerating a capital-flight pattern that began when US-Iran hostilities escalated in March. The Reserve Bank of India has been selling dollars from its reserves to cushion the fall, but traders say the central bank is conserving firepower for a potentially uglier phase ahead.

**Why It Matters Now:** A weaker rupee raises the cost of everything India imports — not just crude, but electronics, edible oils, fertilizers, and gold. Headline inflation, already nudging 5.5%, could breach the RBI’s 6% comfort ceiling within weeks. For Indian corporates with dollar-denominated debt, the depreciation widens repayment burdens at exactly the wrong time.

Prime Minister Modi has responded with a public appeal for fuel conservation and reduced gold purchases — measures that signal the government sees the forex strain as structural rather than transient. The finance ministry is also weighing a fresh sovereign bond issuance targeted at NRI investors, a playbook last used during the 2013 taper tantrum.

**The Diaspora Lens:** For the 4.4 million Indian-Americans sending remittances home, the math has shifted dramatically. A dollar now buys nearly 96 rupees, up from 86 a year ago — meaning every $1,000 wired home converts to roughly 10,000 more rupees than it did twelve months ago. That’s a windfall for families in India, but it also signals genuine economic distress in the home country. NRIs with property investments face a double bind: rental yields look better in dollar terms, but construction costs and loan servicing have risen sharply.

**What to Watch:** The RBI’s next policy meeting on May 22 will be closely scrutinized for any emergency rate action. Analysts project the rupee could test 96.00 if crude stays above $100. The other wildcard: a US-India trade deal, which some officials say could trigger a relief rally if even partial terms are announced during ongoing Section 301 consultations.
nri_angle: The rupee at 95.63 means NRI remittances convert to roughly 10,000 more rupees per $1,000 than a year ago, but the depreciation also erodes the real value of Indian property and investments held by the diaspora.
author: Diaspora Desk
